hmmt-feb-2013-comb-01.title: Count from the first card
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-01.body:
Whatever the first card is, the second card (drawn from the full deck again) must be one of the $12$ other cards of the same suit or one of the $3$ other cards of the same number. Same card (both) is excluded, and a card that shares suit and number with the first is the first card itself. So the probability is $\frac{12+3}{52}=\frac{15}{52}$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{52}$**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-02.title: One equation
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-02.body:
Let $p$ be the probability she sings on Saturday. She can sing on Sunday only if she did not sing on Saturday, which happens with probability $1-p$, and then with chance $0.7$. So $0.7(1-p)=0.5$, giving $p=1-\frac57=\frac27$.

**Answer: $\frac27$**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-03.title: Keep the first of each color
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-03.body:
If all marbles are red, every total is a multiple of $3$, and if all are blue every total is a multiple of $-2$ (never $1$); so he fails in these two cases.

Otherwise both colors appear. Strategy: keep the first red marble and the first blue marble and pass on everything else, for a total of $3-2=1$. This works whenever both colors occur.

So he fails exactly when the marbles are all one color: probability $\frac{2}{2^{2013}}=\frac1{2^{2012}}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{2^{2012}}$**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-04.title: Split into plus and minus groups
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-04.body:
The numbers in odd positions and those in even positions must each sum to $\frac{36}2=18$. Choose the 4-element set containing $1$ with sum $18$: $\{1,2,7,8\},\{1,3,6,8\},\{1,4,5,8\},\{1,4,6,7\}$ (4 sets; check $\{1,5,\ldots\}$ etc. give nothing else). The set containing $1$ can occupy the odd or even positions ($2$ choices), and each group can be arranged in $4!$ ways.

Total: $4\cdot2\cdot4!\cdot4!=4608$.

**Answer: 4608**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-05.title: Count cuts between $1/3$ and $2/3$
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-05.body:
At each step, the color at a given point of a bar flips exactly when the cut position $p$ lies to the right of that point (the left piece is swapped). So the colors at $\frac13$ and $\frac23$ differ after a step exactly when $p\in(\frac13,\frac23)$ (probability $\frac13$), and they stay the same-or-flip together otherwise. Initially the bars are uniform, so the two points agree.

Hence the two points have the same color after $100$ steps iff an even number of the $100$ values of $p$ fall in $(\frac13,\frac23)$. The probability is
$$\sum_{j\text{ even}}\binom{100}{j}\left(\tfrac13\right)^j\left(\tfrac23\right)^{100-j}=\frac12\left[\left(\tfrac23+\tfrac13\right)^{100}+\left(\tfrac23-\tfrac13\right)^{100}\right]=\frac12\left[1+\left(\tfrac13\right)^{100}\right].$$

**Answer: $\frac12\left[\left(\frac13\right)^{100}+1\right]$**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-07.title: Find the worst seed that can win
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-07.body:
Say $x$ vicariously defeats $y$ if $x$ beats $y$ directly or through a chain of wins. A player can beat a player ranked at most $3$ places better, so the seed of the player who (vicariously) beats seed $1$ can climb by at most $3$ each round: $1\to4\to7\to\cdots$. After $2011$ rounds the best possible seed among the semifinalists is at most $3\cdot2011+1=6034$ (seed 1's quarter), and by a similar argument the second semifinalist quarter can have seed at most $6035$ (if seeds 1 and 2 are in different quarters; if in the same quarter, the quarter's winner is at most $6032$, which is worse). The eventual champion must beat the strongest semifinalist and one more, so it is at most $6038$ (e.g. $6034,6035,6036,6038$ in the semifinals). This is achievable by an explicit draw, and swapping seed $6038$ with any better seed $x$ in the draw shows every seed $x\le6038$ can win.

So exactly $6038$ players can win.

**Answer: 6038**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-08.title: Case on how many people the statements are about
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-08.body:
**Statements about 3 different people.** Then either $0$ or $2$ statements accuse; in either case, by symmetry the inspector cannot determine the thief. $0$ triplets.

**Statements about 1 or 2 people.**
- *Two statements equal* (so true, as only one lies; the third is false). If all three are about the same person, there must be $2$ accusations and $1$ claim of innocence (else the other two suspects could not be told apart): $3$ choices of person $\times3$ choices for who says the innocence claim $=9$. If about two different people, the only impossible case is two accusations of one person plus a claim of innocence about another; the possible patterns number $3$, with $6$ ways to pick the people and $3$ ways to assign: $3\cdot6\cdot3=54$.
- *All three statements different*: they must be about two people, with one person $A$ both accused and declared innocent, and a third statement about $B$; this must be an accusation of $B$ (an innocence claim for $B$ leaves two suspects). Choosing $A,B$ ($6$ ways) and who says what ($3!=6$) gives $36$.

Total $9+54+36=99$.

**Answer: 99**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-09.title: Double counting
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-09.body:
$f(\sigma)^4$ counts the quadruples $(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)$ of (not necessarily distinct) fixed points of $\sigma$. Swap the sums: we count pairs $(\sigma,(a_1,\dots,a_4))$ with all $a_i$ fixed.

Suppose a pattern of equalities among the $a_i$ gives $k$ distinct values. There are $2013\cdot2012\cdots(2013-k+1)$ ways to choose the values and $(2013-k)!$ permutations fixing them, so each pattern contributes exactly $2013!$.

The number of equality patterns is the number of set partitions of $4$ elements: $1+7+6+1=15$ (Bell number $B_4$). So the sum is $15\cdot2013!$.

**Answer: $15\cdot2013!$**

hmmt-feb-2013-comb-10.title: Reflection principle
hmmt-feb-2013-comb-10.body:
Let $S=f(2013)$ and $M=\max_{0\le n\le2013}f(n)\ge0$. For $a\ge1$, reflecting the walk after its first visit to level $a$ gives $P(M\ge a)=P(S\ge a)+P(S>a)$. Summing over $a\ge1$ and using $\sum_{a\ge1}P(S\ge a)=E[S^+]$, $\sum_{a\ge1}P(S>a)=E[(S-1)^+]=E[S^+]-P(S>0)$:
$$E[M]=2E[S^+]-P(S>0)=E|S|-\tfrac12,$$
since $S$ is symmetric and never $0$ (2013 is odd), so $E[S^+]=\frac12E|S|$ and $P(S>0)=\frac12$.

For odd $N$ flips, $S=2k-N$ with $k$ heads, and using $k\binom Nk=N\binom{N-1}{k-1}$ and Pascal's rule, $\sum_{k\ge m}(2k-N)\binom Nk=N\sum_{k\ge m}\left[\binom{N-1}{k-1}-\binom{N-1}k\right]=N\binom{N-1}{m-1}$ (telescoping), where $m=\frac{N+1}2$. Hence $E|S|=\frac{2N\binom{N-1}{(N-1)/2}}{2^N}=\frac{N\binom{N-1}{(N-1)/2}}{2^{N-1}}$. For $N=2013$ and $2013\binom{2012}{1006}=1007\binom{2013}{1006}$:
$$E[M]=-\frac12+\frac{1007\binom{2013}{1006}}{2^{2012}}\approx35.3 .$$
(Sanity check with $N=3$ flips: $-\frac12+\frac{2\binom31}{2^2}=1$, and the $8$ paths have maxima $3,2,1,1,1,0,0,0$ with mean $1$.)

**Answer: $-\frac12+\frac{1007\binom{2013}{1006}}{2^{2012}}$**
